title: Spatial Configuration, Organisational Change and Academic Networks

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005 to 2012) with spatial and organizational changes
findings.consequent: Average frequency of face-to-face contact for the whole department
findings.mechanism: Average accessibility increased (mean depth decreased) and numbers of people sharing offices increased.
findings.quote: The average frequency of face-to-face contact for the whole department increased from 2.06 (2005) to 2.66 (2008) and 2.77 (2012)

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005 to 2012) with spatial and organizational changes
findings.consequent: Average perceived usefulness of colleagues for the whole department
findings.mechanism: Average accessibility increased (mean depth decreased) and numbers of people sharing offices increased.
findings.quote: The same effect occurred for average usefulness, which rose from 1.55 to 1.89 and 1.95.

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005 to 2012) with spatial and organizational changes
findings.mechanism: First increased from 0.178 (2005) to 0.231 (2008), then fell to 0.175 (2012).
findings.quote: density of the weekly interaction network first increased from 0.178 (2005) to 0.231 (2008), but then fell to 0.175 (2012).

findings.antecedent: Introduction of a staff and student common room/kitchen/print room on the second floor (2008)
findings.consequent: Average frequency of contact (av_freq) and weekly interaction network density (freq345)
findings.mechanism: The common room served as a social and task-related hub, increasing opportunities for colleagues to see each other.
findings.quote: in 2008 a staff and student common room/kitchen/print room was introduced on the second floor, which was a meeting point for everyone

findings.antecedent: Provision of a kitchen/print room on each of the two floors (2012)
findings.consequent: Density of the weekly interaction network
findings.mechanism: No single meeting point for everyone in the department, reducing opportunities for spontaneous interaction.
findings.quote: In 2012 both floors had its own kitchen / print room, which meant that again there was no single meeting point for everyone

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005 to 2012) with spatial and organizational changes
findings.consequent: Density of network of highly useful colleagues (cumuseGT5)
findings.mechanism: Increasing levels of visibility (decreasing mean depth) could have increased awareness of colleagues and their work; managerial activities and organizational events also had an impact.
findings.quote: density of the network of highly useful colleagues (0.037 → 0.040 → 0.047) can only be speculated upon.

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005 to 2012) with spatial and organizational changes
findings.consequent: Densities of overall contact (freq12345) and usefulness (cumuse) networks
findings.mechanism: More selective interaction and collaboration behavior, with staff interacting with fewer people in total but more intensively with those contacts.
findings.quote: densities of the overall networks of contact and usefulness (freq12345: 0.553 → 0.456 → 0.322 and cumuse: 0.230 → 0.225 → 0.176) continuously decreased

findings.antecedent: Group affiliation
findings.mechanism: Weekly interaction mainly occurred across groups, with 37-47% of ties being group internal.
findings.quote: Weekly interaction mainly occurred across groups, since only 37-47% of ties were group internal.

findings.antecedent: Co-location on the same floor
findings.mechanism: Floor internal ties remained relatively stable from 2005 to 2008, but increased in 2012 with a kitchen/print room on each floor.
findings.quote: Floor internal ties in the weekly interaction network remained relatively stable from 2005 to 2008, but increased again in 2012

findings.antecedent: Group affiliation
findings.mechanism: Daily interaction mainly remained within the group, with group affiliation determining intensity and frequency.
findings.quote: daily interaction mainly remained within the group with a proportion of 54-74%. Therefore, group affiliation determined the intensity and frequency of interaction.

findings.antecedent: Co-location on the same floor
findings.mechanism: Being on the same floor was a consistently strong determinant of who someone saw daily.
findings.quote: For the daily face-to-face interaction network, being on the same floor is a very strong determinant of who someone saw

findings.antecedent: Role (Administrator)
findings.mechanism: Administrators were increasingly seen as useful over time.
findings.quote: administrators were seen as increasingly useful

findings.antecedent: Role (Administrator) and co-location on lower ground floor (2012)
findings.consequent: Average frequency of being seen face-to-face
findings.mechanism: Being located on the lower ground floor cut off administrators from others on the ground floor.
findings.quote: in 2012 almost half of them were located on the lower ground floor, which affected their frequency of being seen face-to-face.

findings.antecedent: Role (Senior academic staff) and deliberate absence/working from elsewhere (2012)
findings.consequent: Average frequency of being seen face-to-face
findings.mechanism: Senior staff working from home or elsewhere after giving up single offices reduced their contact levels.
findings.quote: decreasing levels of contact might also be caused by the deliberate absence and working from elsewhere in 2012

findings.antecedent: Role (PhD student) and allocation to a large, central area in new building (2012)
findings.consequent: Contact frequency and visibility to everyone else
findings.mechanism: Central and large allocation in the new building increased their opportunities for interaction.
findings.quote: PhD students: they were allocated a large and very central area in the new building in 2012 and thus their contact frequency and visibility to everyone else increased.

findings.antecedent: Research group D and complete accommodation on lower ground floor (2012)
findings.mechanism: Being completely on the lower ground floor cut off Group D significantly from others on the ground floor.
findings.quote: frequency of contact for group D in 2012, which decreased against the trend of all other groups.

findings.antecedent: Research group D and complete accommodation on lower ground floor (2012)
findings.mechanism: Despite decreased contact, members of group D were still found highly useful by others.
findings.quote: this did not affect their value to everyone else, since members of group D were still found highly useful

findings.antecedent: Research group C and organisational restructuring (colleagues leaving)
findings.mechanism: Weakening of the group due to closest colleagues leaving for another organizational unit.
findings.quote: group C behaved against the trend and showed lower values of average usefulness than everyone else.

findings.antecedent: Organisational restructuring (colleagues leaving) and spatial accommodation on different floors (2012)
findings.consequent: Internal network density of high usefulness (cumuseGT5) for Group C
findings.mechanism: Departure of colleagues weakened the group, and disjointed parts of the group accommodated on different floors further impacted network structures.
findings.quote: structure of the group in 2012, which changed to more isolates and a core structure of collaborative ties in dyads or triplets.

findings.antecedent: Externally funded research projects and open-plan office space (2012)
findings.consequent: Internal network density of high usefulness (cumuseGT5) for Group B
findings.mechanism: Two externally funded research projects made the group connected in a more equal fashion, supported by a shift to almost everyone in open-plan offices, though density slightly decreased from 0.16 to 0.15.
findings.quote: In 2012 two externally funded research projects made the group connected in a more equal fashion again.

findings.antecedent: Higher seniority (e.g., Professor vs. Lecturer)
findings.consequent: Larger and more heterophilic ego networks
findings.mechanism: Senior people tend to have broader connections and diverse contacts.
findings.quote: The more senior people tend to have larger and more heterophilic networks.

findings.antecedent: Higher seniority (e.g., Professor vs. Lecturer)
findings.consequent: Higher centrality (betweenness) in their own ego networks
findings.mechanism: Senior people often act as bridges, connecting researchers around them.
findings.quote: They also tend to be more central in their own ego networks, i.e. they connect the researchers around them

findings.antecedent: Career advancement
findings.mechanism: As academics advance, their professional connections and collaborations tend to expand.
findings.quote: As academics advance in their career, ego networks grow: for instance the network of person E grew from 6 to 9 to 8.

findings.antecedent: Career advancement
findings.mechanism: Academics establish diverse agendas, research topics, and networks as they gain seniority.
findings.quote: Ego networks also diversify with career advancement, for instance network homophily decreased for person D from 75% in 2005 to 40% in 2012

findings.antecedent: Departure of important colleagues/collaborators (organizational change)
findings.mechanism: The loss of close collaborators due to organizational restructuring severely impacted Person C's network within the department.
findings.quote: most severe impact on person C, whose network within the department shrank dramatically

findings.antecedent: Office type or location (spatial configuration)
findings.mechanism: Neither office type nor location (as measured by accessibility) displayed a consistent pattern in shaping individual ego-networks.
findings.quote: it can be observed that space did not play a major role for the structure of ego-networks. Neither office type nor location (as measured by accessibility) seems to display any single pattern.

findings.antecedent: Spatial configuration (e.g., common room, floor co-location)
findings.mechanism: Space manages proximity and distance, bringing people together or keeping them apart, influencing collective interaction patterns.
findings.quote: spatial configuration is an important driver of academic networks of collaboration

findings.antecedent: Spatial configuration
findings.mechanism: The impact of space on social existence lies in the relations between configurations of people and configurations of space, not at the individual level.
findings.quote: On the level of individual people and the structures of their ego networks, however, no clear impact of space could be identified.

stimuli.description: Office layouts (single, double/triple cellular, group, open-plan), common rooms, kitchen/print facilities, overall building configuration (mean depth, visibility) across three time points (2005, 2008, 2012).

tables.description: Overview of minimum, average and maximum mean depth figures for visibility and accessibility models of the spatial network of the department in 2005, 2008 and 2012
Average figures of frequency of being seen and perceived usefulness for all staff as well as network densities of the department in 2005, 2008 and 2012
Overview of E-I index calculation results of weekly and daily interaction networks in 2005, 2008 and 2012 using both research group affiliation and floor of office location as category
Spatial information and metrics as well as network metrics of the ego networks of six selected academics over the years

limitations: The case study may have not been ideally suited to draw conclusions on the distinct roles of space and organisation in shaping academic collaborative networks within an organisation because the organisation changed too much in between the three points in time, so that in effect both variables, space and organisation changed, making it difficult to come to conclusive results.
